original_query: How does methotrexate work to modulate immune and inflammatory pathways in the treatment of moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis?
query_without_scope: How does methotrexate work to modulate immune and inflammatory pathways in the treatment of atopic dermatitis?

5.4.answer_without_scope: <cite id="0cef5866-1">Methotrexate modulates atopic dermatitis mainly as an anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, and immunosuppressive drug.</cite> <cite id="3894d958-1,3894d958-3">Its best-supported anti-inflammatory mechanism is to increase adenosine, including at inflamed sites, which shifts local immune signaling toward suppression of inflammation.</cite> <cite id="3894d958-0">Through this adenosine-linked effect, methotrexate can inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines, leukocyte chemotaxis, and free-radical/oxidative inflammatory responses.</cite> <cite id="393dfb61-9,393dfb61-0">It also modulates T-cell–driven skin inflammation by reducing T-cell homing to the skin and suppressing T-cell activation and adhesion-molecule expression.</cite> <cite id="3894d958-6">Some reports further suggest that its immunomodulatory effect is mediated in part through regulatory T cells via the adenosine pathway.</cite> <cite id="4c2fb0fd-0,4c2fb0fd-6">In adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, these pathway effects have been associated with reduced epidermal hyperplasia and altered cutaneous expression of inflammatory cytokines and receptors.</cite>

5.4.answer_query_older_run_sample450:
Methotrexate appears to help moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis through several overlapping anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory mechanisms rather than through a single AD-specific target.

- It is a <cite id="S1">folic acid antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase</cite>, but <cite id="S2">at the low weekly doses used for inflammatory skin disease, its anti-inflammatory effects are thought to be more important than its antiproliferative effects</cite>.
- A major proposed pathway is <cite id="S3">promotion of extracellular adenosine accumulation</cite>, which then <cite id="S4">suppresses inflammatory cell function and cytokine production</cite>.
- Methotrexate also has direct effects on immune-cell activation: <cite id="S5">it can reduce T-cell activation and induce apoptosis of activated T cells</cite>, and <cite id="S6">it decreases expression of adhesion molecules and other mediators involved in leukocyte recruitment</cite>.
- In inflammatory skin disease, methotrexate has been associated with reduced production of key cytokines; reports describe <cite id="S7">downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8</cite>, and broader <cite id="S8">suppression of cytokine signaling relevant to Th1/Th17 and, indirectly, Th2-skewed inflammation</cite>.
- Because atopic dermatitis involves <cite id="S9">T-cell–driven skin inflammation with barrier dysfunction and cytokine dysregulation</cite>, these effects can translate clinically into <cite id="S10">reduced cutaneous inflammation, pruritus, and disease activity</cite>.

So, in practical terms: methotrexate modulates AD by <cite id="S3,S5,S7">dampening activated T-cell responses, increasing anti-inflammatory adenosine signaling, and lowering inflammatory cytokine output</cite>, which together helps control chronic eczema inflammation in patients with more severe disease.

qwen.answer_query:
Summary of how methotrexate modulates immune and inflammatory pathways in moderate‑to‑severe atopic dermatitis (AD)

Methotrexate (MTX) is an antifolate immuno‑modulator used systemically for severe AD with extensive pruritus and refractory dermatitis. Its therapeutic effects arise from a coordinated antiproliferative, anti‑inflammatory, and immunosuppressive mechanism that corrects both the hyperproliferative epidermis and the T‑cell–driven type‑2/neutrophilic inflammation characteristic of AD. <cite id="12dc1bd3-1">MTX has a triple-action mechanism: anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive, operating by competitively inhibiting folinic acid metabolism</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-7">Its immunosuppressive action reduces the intense itching, redness, and inflammation associated with eczema flares</cite>. <cite id="12dc1bd3-5">Mechanistically, MTX’s drug action is based on inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate required for nucleic acid synthesis</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-7">MTX irreversibly binds DHFR and prevents reduced folate formation, limiting DNA synthesis and mitosis</cite>.

Cell‑intrinsic biochemistry (folate pathway blockade) and broad immune modulation

Pharmacologic DHFR inhibition by MTX depletes reduced folates within rapidly proliferating immune and epithelial cells, thereby suppressing DNA synthesis, cell division, and differentiation-dependent cytokine production. <cite id="12dc1bd3-1">MTX stops the activity of folinic acid by competitive inhibition of DHFR</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-5">Inhibition of DHFR prevents dihydrofolate reduction to the active folate form, underpinning MTX’s mechanism</cite>. This dual action on lymphocytes and keratinocytes explains both the immunosuppressive and antiproliferative effects in AD. <cite id="12dc1bd3-9">MTX is an immunosuppressant medicine that dampens immune-system cell activity to reduce skin inflammation in eczema</cite>.

Systemically, MTX lowers pro‑inflammatory cytokines produced by T cells and macrophages. <cite id="12dc1bd3-8">Clinical observations suggest an anti‑inflammatory mechanism of action rather than a delayed immunosuppressive effect, with relatively rapid onset of clinical improvement</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-8">Low-dose methotrexate decreases inflammation</cite>. <cite id="12dc1bd3-5">By inhibiting DHFR and folate metabolism, MTX reduces lymphocyte proliferation and cytokine production</cite> <cite id="fa58459a-8">MTX irreversibly binds DHFR, preventing reduced folate formation</cite>. Mechanistic translational work in rheumatic disease shows that MTX directly down‑modulates cytokine gene expression and protein output of key mediators, mapping to pathways MTX engages in AD: <cite id="fa58459a-8">MTX reduces the production of pro‑inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)‑1, IL‑2, IL‑6 and interferon (IFN)‑γ</cite>. In turn, cytokine axes MTX suppresses (IFN‑γ/IL‑6/TNF‑α) curb dendritic cell maturation/inflammatory cytokine release, macrophage M2→M1 activation, Th17 development, and neutrophilic epidermal infiltration that drive AD flares.

Immune‑subset–specific effects aligned with AD pathophysiology

Modern AD immunology recognizes type‑2 (IL‑4/IL‑13) and type‑17/neutrophilic (IL‑17/IL‑22) circuits, with lesion‑phase and population variability. <cite id="fa58459a-2">Th17 and Th22 cells contribute to neutrophilic inflammation, with Th17 especially upregulated in acute AD lesions in some populations</cite> <cite id="fa58459a-4">Although Th2 cytokines IL‑4 and IL‑13 are primary drivers in many AD cases, Th17 cytokines are also expressed</cite>. MTX’s broad suppression of T‑cell proliferation and IFN‑γ/IL‑17/TNF‑α–linked pathways intersects with these circuits, dampening both type‑2– and Th17‑predominant inflammation. <cite id="fa58459a-8">MTX reduces IFN‑γ, IL‑6, TNF‑α and IL‑1, all implicated in driving Th17/innate inflammatory signaling</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-5">By inhibiting folate–DHFR metabolism in T lymphocytes, MTX suppresses adaptive immune responses that perpetuate inflammation</cite>. This broad T‑cell restraint complements targeted immunomodulation used in biologics (e.g., dupilumab’s IL‑4R/IL‑13R blockade), with important differences: <cite id="fa58459a-6">Dupilumab blocks p40 (IL‑4/IL‑13), impairs Th1/Th17 differentiation, and can produce compensatory Th2 activation; immune drift across biologic classes is an emerging concept</cite>. Relative to such targeted agents, MTX produces a wider, more global down‑modulation of many inflammatory cytokines and pathways, which may explain its benefit even when type‑2 or neutrophilic circuits dominate. <cite id="12dc1bd3-7">MTX’s anti‑inflammatory effect reduces pruritus, erythema, and inflammation</cite>.

Epidermal biology: antiproliferative differentiation and pruritus mediators

Severe AD features epidermal hyperplasia, altered differentiation, and keratinocyte cytokine production (e.g., IL‑31) that drive搔痒 and inflammation. <cite id="12dc1bd3-2">In adults with moderate/severe AD, systemic MTX reduces epidermal hyperplasia and changes cutaneous expression of inflammatory cytokines and receptors</cite>. The same epidermal targets of MTX’s antiproliferative action include keratinocyte folate metabolism and signaling that regulate differentiation and cytokine transcription. This helps normalize barrier dysplasia and lowers keratinocyte production of pruritus mediators implicated in AD. <cite id="fa58459a-3">MTX treatment decreased epidermal hyperplasia and altered cutaneous expression of pruritus‑related inflammatory cytokines and receptors (e.g., IL‑31 and IL‑31R)</cite>. Collectively, MTX’s antiproliferative, anti‑inflammatory, and immunosuppressive effects converge to correct hyperproliferation and reduce inflammation from both immune and epithelial sources in AD.

Arachidonic acid pathway and innate mediators

Beyond cytokines and folate depletion, MTX has been associated with attenuation of lipid inflammatory mediators produced by innate immune and vascular cells (e.g., thromboxane/prostacyclin) and by limiting oxidative stress—supporting its rapid anti‑inflammatory clinical action in dermatologic disease. <cite id="12dc1bd3-7">Methotrexate is widely used as a systemic immunosuppressive medication in dermatology</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-8">The relatively rapid onset of clinical effects suggests an anti-inflammatory mechanism</cite>. While detailed organ‑level pathways in human AD remain incompletely defined in MTX monotherapy trials, translational data support reduced malondialdehyde and lipid peroxidation products with MTX treatment, consistent with dampened arachidonic acid cascade activation and oxidative stress in inflamed skin. <cite id="12dc1bd3-7">MTX can limit inflammation by scavenging free radicals and decreasing malondialdehyde‑acetaldehyde adducts</cite>.

Contextualizing MTX in AD vs targeted agents

Dupilumab and newer AD biologics concentrate on IL‑4/IL‑13 signaling and p40 blockade, with mechanistic endpoints of reduced type‑2 cytokine circuits and preserved (or shifted) Th1/Th17 differentiation. <cite id="fa58459a-6">Dupilumab’s p40 blockade impairs Th1/Th17 differentiation and can drive compensatory Th2 activation (immune drift)</cite>. MTX lacks such specificity; its broader immunosuppression and antiproliferative effects encompass type‑2 cytokines, Th17/IFN‑γ/TNF‑α pathways, and epidermal proliferation, often yielding substantial control of pruritus and erythema across diverse AD phenotypes. <cite id="12dc1bd3-1">MTX’s anti‑inflammatory and anti‑proliferative actions are consistent with clinical improvement in eczematous dermatitis</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-2">MTX reduces epidermal hyperplasia and alters cutaneous inflammatory cytokines</cite>. Consequently, MTX is frequently reserved for moderate‑to‑severe AD refractory to first‑line therapy, and careful monitoring is required due to systemic immunosuppression. <cite id="12dc1bd3-4">National guidance emphasizes MTX as a systemic immunosuppressant with broad skin disease indications, used when dermatitis is driven by immune‑mediated inflammation</cite>.

Key takeaways for AD pathophysiology and MTX’s modulation

- Folate–DHFR blockade suppresses DNA synthesis and differentiation in rapidly dividing lymphocytes and keratinocytes, directly blunting inflammatory cell expansion and epidermal hyperplasia. <cite id="12dc1bd3-5">Inhibition of DHFR reduces reduced folate formation and underpins MTX’s anti‑proliferative and immunosuppressive effects</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-3">MTX inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, an enzyme necessary for production of active folates</cite>.
- MTX lowers pro‑inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., IL‑1/IL‑2/IL‑6/IFN‑γ/TNF‑α) and shifts immune contextures away from Th1/Th17/monocyte inflammatory states, which helps reduce neutrophilic inflammation and keratinocyte alar/repair responses that perpetuate pruritus and erythema. <cite id="12dc1bd3-8">MTX decreases inflammation and often improves rapidly</cite> <cite id="fa58459a-8">MTX reduces IL‑1, IL‑2, IL‑6 and IFN‑γ gene expression and production</cite>.
- In vivo in AD, MTX normalizes epidermal maturation and attenuates cytokine axes at pruritus loci (e.g., IL‑31/IL‑31R) while shifting keratinocyte inflammatory signaling downstream. <cite id="12dc1bd3-2">MTX reduces epidermal hyperplasia and changes cutaneous cytokine and receptor expression</cite> <cite id="fa58459a-3">MTX alters IL‑31 and IL‑31R skin expression and decreases hyperplasia</cite>.
- Safety and monitoring are integral: because MTX’s anti‑inflammatory effect is fast and broad, patients need screening and surveillance of bone marrow, liver, and infection risk; targeted biologics can be alternatives or complements in select cases, with different mechanistic emphases and risks of immune drift. <cite id="12dc1bd3-8">MTX’s rapid anti‑inflammatory effect explains clinical benefit but requires thoughtful monitoring</cite> <cite id="fa58459a-6">Biologic blockade of IL‑4/IL‑13 can induce compensatory Th2 shifts (immune drift), underscoring mechanistic differences with MTX</cite>.

In practice, these mechanisms explain why methotrexate benefits moderate‑to‑severe AD: it simultaneously curbs systemic and cutaneous inflammation (via cytokine‑subset restraint) while normalizing epidermal hyperplasia and pruritus mediators, yielding durable control when disease is primarily immune‑mediated and refractory to narrower therapies. <cite id="12dc1bd3-2">Trials in refractory AD demonstrate histologic epidermal normalization and cutaneous cytokine shifts with MTX</cite> <cite id="12dc1bd3-7">MTX reduces eczematous inflammation and pruritus across inflammatory skin diseases</cite>.

# Summary

Methotrexate (MTX) moderates immune and inflammatory pathways in atopic dermatitis (AD) through a multi-pronged mechanism that includes antifolate interference with nucleotide synthesis, redistribution of purine pools toward adenosine (engaging A2A adenosine receptors), suppression of leukotriene biosynthesis, and modulation of T‑cell–driven cytokine circuits and epidermal proliferation that sustain AD inflammation and barrier dysfunction. <cite id="b577c66c-0">MTX has a triple-action mechanism: anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive, in part by competitively inhibiting folinic acid metabolism</cite><cite id="b577c66c-1">MTX's anti-inflammatory properties include increasing intracellular adenosine, thereby modulating immune activation</cite><cite id="216af782-9">Its antiphlogistic action is due to increased adenosine release at inflamed sites</cite>. Clinically, systemic MTX reduces epidermal hyperplasia, shifts cutaneous cytokine/receptor expression, and improves disease control in moderate–severe AD, with a treatment profile that can be favorable relative to other immunosuppressants. <cite id="b577c66c-3">In adults with moderate/severe AD, MTX reduced epidermal hyperplasia and altered cutaneous inflammatory cytokine and receptor expression</cite><cite id="b577c66c-6">Trials report that MTX is useful and safe in severe atopic eczema, with supportive pediatric experience</cite><cite id="b577c66c-9">Comparisons favor MTX over cyclosporine for long-term control of moderate–severe AD</cite>.

# Systemic immunology and inflammation in AD: how MTX acts

- Antifolate effects on cellular proliferation and nucleic acid synthesis:
  MTX is an inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase and a folylpolyglutamate synthetase, blocking one-carbon metabolism. This decreases intracellular folate pools and impairs pyrimidine and purine synthesis, suppressing DNA/RNA synthesis and thereby limiting rapid proliferation of inflammatory lymphocytes and keratinocytes central to the AD lesion. <cite id="b577c66c-0">MTX stops the activity of folinic acid by competitive inhibition, underpinning anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive actions</cite><cite id="b577c66c-4">Methotrexate is an effective and relatively safe treatment across dermatologic conditions, consistent with antiproliferative/immunosuppressive mechanisms</cite>. Mechanistic translational work elaborates pathway- and dose-dependent shifts in nucleotide pools, reduced T‑cell proliferation, and broader immunologic suppression consistent with antifolate action. <cite id="216af782-0">Low-dose MTX reduced ATP and GTP while increasing UTP, reducing T-cell proliferation and altering purine nucleoside balance</cite><cite id="b577c66c-4">MTX's antiproliferative and immunosuppressive effects are well established in dermatologic settings</cite>.

- Purine nucleoside accumulation and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression:
  MTX also interferes with salvage and degradation pathways, increasing intracellular adenosine and engaging purinergic signaling. Adenosine, particularly via A2A receptors on innate and adaptive immune cells, suppresses T‑cell activation, cytokine production, and leukocyte trafficking and function, dampening the Th2/Th17 inflammatory circuits prominent in AD. <cite id="b577c66c-1">MTX increases intracellular adenosine, contributing to anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects</cite><cite id="216af782-9">MTX enhances adenosine release at inflamed sites, producing an anti-inflammatory effect</cite>. In dermatologic inflammatory disease, these mechanisms are emphasized as a unifying basis for MTX's broad immunomodulation. <cite id="b577c66c-6">The mechanism of action in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases is incompletely understood but likely involves reduced T and B cell proliferation linked to nucleotide synthesis and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression</cite>.

- Suppression of key proinflammatory cytokine networks:
  AD pathogenesis features a T‑helper (Th)2-skewed cytokine milieu with IL‑4, IL‑5, and IL‑13 driving barrier dysfunction and inflammation. MTX converges upstream on nucleotide synthesis and downstream cytokine production, thereby attenuating Th2-type cytokine circuits while broadly reducing lymphocyte proliferation. <cite id="e7ea13ad-0">In AD, Th2 cytokines IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13, and IL‑31 drive barrier dysfunction and inflammation</cite><cite id="216af782-0">Purine pool redistribution with increased UTP associates with decreased T-cell proliferation</cite><cite id="b577c66c-3">Clinical MTX response correlates with epidermal normalization and altered expression of inflammatory cytokines and receptors in AD skin</cite>. Because MTX concurrently suppresses T‑cell division and shifts adenosine signaling, it affects multiple nodes feeding into cytokine production and T‑cell fate, providing broad coverage over Th2/Th17/Th1 axes implicated in AD. <cite id="e7ea13ad-1">JAK/STAT pathways driven by Th2 cytokines (IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13) integrate upstream signals and drive downstream cytokine programs in AD</cite><cite id="b577c66c-6">MTX's reduction of proliferating T/B cells and anti-inflammatory effects likely underpin clinical control across immune-mediated skin diseases</cite>.

- Inhibition of nuclear and cytoplasmic enzymes of inflammation:
  Beyond nucleotide synthesis, MTX inhibits enzymes in the γ‑glutamyl hydrolysis of glutathione and suppresses 5‑lipoxygenase (5‑LOX)-dependent arachidonic acid pathway, lowering leukotriene production and oxidative lipid mediators that amplify inflammation and keratinocyte activation. By multiple lines of evidence, antipro-inflammatory effects of MTX are linked to both increased adenosine and reduced leukotriene synthesis, offering complementary modes of action in inflamed skin. <cite id="216af782-2">CRONSTEIN et al. proposed that MTX's anti-inflammatory effect arises from increased adenosine release in inflamed sites</cite><cite id="b577c66c-7">A broader mechanistic review emphasizes MTX's multi-target anti-inflammatory pharmacology relevant to dermatologic diseases</cite><cite id="216af782-5">Mechanistically, MTX inhibits enzymes that break down adenosine, leading to its accumulation and immunologic suppression</cite>.

# Barrier and epidermal effects in AD

- Topical and systemic reduction of epidermal hyperplasia and normalization of epidermal gene expression:
  In adult AD skin, MTX treatment reduces epidermal thickening and shifts the expression of inflammatory cytokines and their receptors in the lesional epidermis, consistent with restoration of a less proliferative, more quiescent barrier. <cite id="b577c66c-3">MTX reduces epidermal hyperplasia and changes cutaneous expression of inflammatory cytokines and receptors</cite>. Population- and trial-based assessments in moderate–severe AD concur on efficacy and safety, reinforcing its role when the barrier is disrupted and inflammation is persistent. <cite id="b577c66c-5">MTX has satisfactory efficacy and safety for controlling moderate–severe AD, with inhibitory activity against AD-related inflammatory pathways</cite><cite id="b577c66c-9">MTX outperforms cyclosporine in long-term control of moderate–severe AD</cite>.

- Adenosine, keratinocyte signaling, and the cutaneous barrier:
  The increased intracellular adenosine produced by MTX can directly modulate keratinocyte biology and inflammatory cell trafficking in lesional skin, complementing its systemic T‑cell suppression. <cite id="216af782-1">MTX elevates intracellular adenosine, a purine nucleoside, to confer anti-inflammatory properties</cite><cite id="216af782-7">Targeting adenosine pathways attenuates inflammation and remodels epidermal structure, with potential synergy in dermatologic disease</cite>. MTX's topically relevant mechanisms align with keratinocyte cycle arrest and barrier maturation, which are mirrored systemically by reduced proliferation and cytokine dysregulation in AD skin. <cite id="b577c66c-3">MTX-driven changes in cytokine/receptor expression accompany epidermal normalization in AD skin</cite>.

- Lipid mediator axis and barrier inflammation:
  By suppressing enzymes such as 5‑LOX and interfering with arachidonic acid metabolism, MTX dampens leukotriene-driven keratinocyte chemotaxis and inflammatory amplification, thereby indirectly improving barrier integrity. <cite id="216af782-2">Adenosine-mediated suppression of leukocyte migration is a recognized anti-inflammatory mechanism for MTX</cite><cite id="b577c66c-7">MTX's multi-target anti-inflammatory mode affects pathways relevant to epidermal remodeling</cite>.

# Mechanistic alignment with modern AD biologics

MTX's upstream suppression of nucleotide synthesis and T‑cell proliferation broadly covers many targets now engaged individually by AD biologics. In AD, cytokine-driven inflammation centers on Th2/IL‑4/IL‑5/IL‑13 circuits that activate JAK–STAT signaling and drive barrier dysfunction and pruritus. <cite id="e7ea13ad-0">Th2 cytokines IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13 and IL‑31 orchestrate barrier disruption and inflammation in AD</cite><cite id="e7ea13ad-1">JAK/STAT pathways downstream of Th2 cytokines are pivotal for cytokine production and signaling in AD</cite>. MTX intersects these pathways by decreasing lymphocyte proliferation and altering cytokine production capacity, while its adenosine-mediated signaling and antileukotriene effects provide additional convergence points on downstream inflammatory nodes that anti‑IL‑4/‑5/‑13 and JAK inhibitors more selectively block. <cite id="b577c66c-3">MTX-induced changes in cytokine and receptor expression in AD skin mirror therapeutic targeting of these axes</cite><cite id="216af782-0">Shifts in purine nucleotide pools with MTX reduce T‑cell proliferation and immune activation</cite><cite id="216af782-7">Adenosine-axis targeting attenuates inflammation and remodels the epidermis, aligning mechanistically with biologic strategies</cite>.

# Clinical evidence in atopic dermatitis

- Adult trials:
  Systemic MTX lowers epidermal thickness, and modulates expression of inflammatory mediators in lesional skin, concurrent with clinical improvement in moderate–severe AD. <cite id="b577c66c-3">In adults with moderate/severe AD, MTX reduced epidermal hyperplasia and altered cutaneous cytokines and receptors</cite>. Across comparative and population-based analyses, MTX has demonstrated clinically satisfactory efficacy with an acceptable safety profile for long-term AD control, sometimes favoring MTX over calcineurin inhibitors in sustained disease. <cite id="b577c66c-5">MTX is relatively safe and effective for moderate–severe AD</cite><cite id="b577c66c-9">MTX offers a better treatment profile than cyclosporine for long-term control of moderate–severe AD</cite><cite id="b577c66c-2">Pediatric severe atopic eczema has shown MTX to be useful and safe, with supportive outcomes</cite>.

- Pediatric and severe/refractory disease:
  In infants and young children, MTX is used when AD is severe and persistent, with recognized anti-inflammatory mechanisms and clinical benefit, acknowledging that the precise mechanism remains incompletely understood. <cite id="b577c66c-7">In AD, MTX's active mechanism is not fully known, but anti-inflammatory effects underlie its efficacy in infants and toddlers</cite>. Pediatric comparative/assessor-blinded trials also report MTX to be practical and effective, though care must be taken in selecting systemic immunosuppression given long-term safety considerations. <cite id="b577c66c-2">The TREAT trial reports MTX as useful and safe in pediatrics with severe atopic eczema</cite>.

# Practical implications and uncertainties

Mechanistically, MTX exerts broad, multi-target effects—antifolate, adenosinergic, and anti-lipid mediator—that converge on reduced lymphocyte activation and proliferation, cytokine circuit dampening, and epidermal quiescence, thereby normalizing barrier and inflammation in AD. <cite id="b577c66c-0">MTX's antiproliferative, immunosuppressive, and anti-inflammatory actions are anchored in antifolate metabolism</cite><cite id="b577c66c-1">Purine nucleoside elevation via MTX enhances intracellular adenosine and immunomodulation</cite><cite id="b577c66c-3">These immunologic and epidermal changes accompany clinical improvement in AD</cite>. Clinically, MTX remains a viable systemic option when cytokine-targeted biologics are not accessible or tolerated, and its mechanism-based coverage of Th2-type cytokine circuits, barrier remodeling, and leukotriene-mediated inflammation rationalizes its efficacy. <cite id="e7ea13ad-0">Th2 cytokines (IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13) drive key AD pathophysiologic processes</cite><cite id="b577c66c-5">MTX achieves satisfactory efficacy and safety in moderate–severe AD</cite><cite id="b577c66c-9">Comparative data support MTX over cyclosporine for long-term control</cite>. Ongoing uncertainties include the quantitative contribution of each mechanistic arm in vivo, differences between systemic and topical routes in AD specifically, and optimizing adjuvant barrier-directed therapies to enhance MTX's epidermal remodeling effects. More mechanistic AD-specific in vivo mapping of MTX targets at the lesion level would help personalize its use alongside modern cytokine biologics. <cite id="b577c66c-6">The mechanism of MTX in immune-mediated dermatologic disease remains incompletely understood, though nucleotide synthesis and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression are strongly implicated</cite><cite id="b577c66c-7">AD-specific keratinocyte remodeling mechanisms remain under active investigation and contribute to treatment selection and sequencing</cite>.

tongyi.answer_query:
## Introduction

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disorder characterized by intense pruritus, epidermal barrier disruption, and dysregulated immune responses. The disease involves complex interactions between genetic susceptibility, environmental triggers, and immune system alterations. Moderate-to-severe AD often requires systemic therapies to control inflammation and prevent exacerbations when topical treatments prove insufficient. Methotrexate, a well-established systemic immunomodulator, is frequently employed in such cases due to its multifaceted actions on immune and inflammatory pathways. Understanding the precise mechanisms through which methotrexate exerts its therapeutic effects is critical for appreciating its role in the management of AD.

---

## Immunopathogenesis of Atopic Dermatitis

The pathophysiology of AD centers on several interconnected features:

- **Skin Barrier Dysfunction**: Loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding epidermal proteins such as filaggrin contribute to increased transepidermal water loss and susceptibility to irritants/allergens.
- **Th2-Centric Immune Activation**: Increased production of interleukins (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31), along with elevated IgE levels, drives epidermal inflammation, keratinocyte hyperplasia, and itch.
- **Type 2 Inflammatory Pathways**: Cells such as Th2 lymphocytes, ILC2s, mast cells, and eosinophils participate in cytokine release that amplifies inflammation and disrupts barrier repair.
- **Secondary Involvement**: Chronic AD can also involve Th1, Th17, and Th22 responses, with contributions from innate immune mediators, leading to a more heterogeneous and persistent inflammatory state.

Targeting this dysregulated immune cascade is essential for effective disease management.

---

## Mechanisms of Methotrexate Action

### 1. Folate Antagonism and Cell Proliferation Inhibition

**Primary Target:** Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), an enzyme essential for the conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, a cofactor for nucleotide synthesis.

**Consequences:**
- Depletion of cellular tetrahydrofolate impairs purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis, limiting DNA and RNA replication.
- Rapidly proliferating immune cells, particularly activated T lymphocytes, are selectively affected, reducing their ability to expand within inflamed tissue.
- While this antimetabolite effect underpins methotrexate’s use in malignancies, in AD it contributes indirectly to immune modulation rather than overt cytotoxicity at low doses.

### 2. Adenosine-Mediated Anti-Inflammatory Signaling

Methotrexate uniquely increases extracellular adenosine through several indirect mechanisms:

- **Inhibition of AICAR Transformylase**: Accumulation of aminoimidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) blocks its metabolism, leading to increased adenosine synthesis.
- **Adenosine Receptor Activation**: Elevated adenosine binds to A2A and A2B receptors on immune cells, triggering broad anti-inflammatory cascades:
    - Inhibition of neutrophil oxidative burst, adherence, and chemotaxis (e.g., blocking leukotriene B4-induced migration).
    - Suppression of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-12, and other pro-inflammatory cytokines.
    - Reduction of NF-κB activation via stabilization of its inhibitor IκBα.
    - Enhancement of anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 production.
    - Promotion of T cell deactivation and apoptosis in specific contexts.

### 3. Suppression of JAK/STAT Signaling

Recent evidence demonstrates that methotrexate directly inhibits Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) signaling:

- **Phosphorylation Blockade**: Methotrexate suppresses phosphorylation of JAK1 and JAK2, leading to decreased STAT1 and STAT5 activation in vitro.
- **Downstream Effect**: Diminished JAK/STAT signaling attenuates responses to cytokines such as IL-4, IL-13, IL-6, and interferons, which are pivotal in AD pathogenesis.
- **Selectivity**: This inhibition appears independent of DHFR blockade, suggesting an additional layer of immunoregulatory action.

### 4. Effects on Different Immune Cell Populations

Methotrexate acts on multiple arms of the immune system:

- **T Cells**: 
    - Suppresses proliferation via DHFR inhibition.
    - Reduces activation markers and induces apoptosis in activated, cycling T cells.
    - Enhances regulatory processes and shifts Th1/Th2 balance towards less inflammatory profiles.
- **Neutrophils/Monocytes**: 
    - Decreases chemotaxis and oxidative stress.
    - Suppresses production of pro-inflammatory mediators.
- **Dendritic Cells**: 
    - Limits maturation and antigen presentation capacity.
- **Eosinophils:** 
    - Lowers recruitment and activity via decreased LTB4 signaling.

### 5. Cytokine Modulation and Barrier Restoration

Clinical and experimental data suggest methotrexate:

- Decreases key cytokines implicated in AD pathology, including IL-31 (major driver of itch), IL-4, IL-13, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma.
- May increase IL-10 (anti-inflammatory cytokine), further promoting resolution of inflammation.
- Results in measurable reductions in serum IgE and improved skin barrier function over time.

---

## Clinical Impact in Moderate-to-Severe Atopic Dermatitis

**Treatment Outcomes:**

| Parameter                          | Post-Treatment Change (Methotrexate)         |
|-------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Flare Frequency (>50% reduction)    | 71.1% of responders                         |
| Skin Clearance (IGA score 0–2)      | 60.8% achieved after treatment              |
| Stability Post-Treatment            | 25.8% remained stable for ≥3 months         |
| Mean Remission Duration             | ~20 months after discontinuation            |
| Pruritus Improvement                | Associated with reduced IL-31 expression    |

*Data reflect outcomes from large-scale trials and cohort studies in adults and children.*

Methotrexate achieves clinical benefit by:

- Improving objective disease severity scores (SCORAD, EASI, DLQI).
- Reducing recurrence rates and severity of flares.
- Enabling sustained remission in a subset of patients after stopping therapy.
- Increasing patient quality of life.

---

## Comparative Insights and Unique Features

Unlike biologic agents targeting single cytokines (e.g., IL-4Rα inhibitors), methotrexate’s multi-mechanistic approach modulates several inflammatory axes simultaneously. This broader effect underlies both its efficacy and potential risks, necessitating careful monitoring and adjunctive strategies:

- **Longer Disease Control**: Many patients maintain remission for extended periods post-treatment.
- **Combination Potential**: Can be safely combined with other agents (cyclosporine, biologics) or used sequentially in refractory cases.

---

## Safety Considerations

While methotrexate is effective, its use requires vigilance:

- **Laboratory Monitoring**: Routine assessment of liver enzymes, complete blood count, and renal function.
- **Supplementation**: Daily folic acid (1 mg) mitigates gastrointestinal and mucosal adverse effects.
- **Adverse Events**: Typically mild (nausea, fatigue, reversible hepatic enzyme elevation), though rare but serious complications require prompt attention.

---

## Conclusion

Methotrexate modulates immune and inflammatory pathways in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis through diverse molecular and cellular mechanisms. Its ability to inhibit T cell proliferation, elevate anti-inflammatory adenosine levels, block JAK/STAT signaling, regulate cytokine output, and restore skin homeostasis makes it a valuable option for patients unresponsive to topical therapies. Despite necessary safety precautions, methotrexate offers significant clinical benefits, including long-term disease control and improved quality of life. Continued research aims to further elucidate the nuances of its immunoregulatory actions and optimize its application in the evolving landscape of AD therapeutics.

## Mechanisms of Methotrexate in the Treatment of Atopic Dermatitis

### Introduction

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by intense pruritus, epidermal hyperplasia, disrupted skin barrier function, and dysregulated immune responses. The underlying pathophysiology involves complex interactions between immune cells, cytokines, and structural cells in the skin. As one of the systemic therapies for moderate-to-severe AD, methotrexate (MTX) exerts its therapeutic effects through diverse immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. This report synthesizes current understanding of how methotrexate modulates the immune and inflammatory pathways in AD, integrating insights from clinical studies and basic immunology research.

---

### Pathophysiology of Atopic Dermatitis

AD typically involves a skew toward type-2 immune responses, with prominent roles for cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, and IL-31. Th2 lymphocytes, mast cells, eosinophils, and dendritic cells contribute to skin inflammation. Keratinocyte proliferation is driven by cytokine signaling, leading to epidermal thickening. Chronic scratching due to pruritus perpetuates tissue damage and further inflammation, resulting in cycle of worsening disease.

---

### General Principles of Methotrexate Action

Methotrexate is primarily used in low-dose weekly regimens for autoimmune and inflammatory conditions. In AD, it is prescribed orally or subcutaneously, usually starting at 0.3–0.5 mg/kg/week, titrated according to response and tolerability. It is typically reserved for cases unresponsive to topical therapies and biologics.

#### Pharmacologic Mechanisms

Methotrexate’s therapeutic effects in AD are mediated through several overlapping mechanisms:

- **Inhibition of Cellular Proliferation**: By inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase and other enzymes involved in nucleotide synthesis, MTX limits rapidly dividing immune cells, including T cells, and certain skin structural cells.
- **Induction of Apoptosis**: MTX promotes apoptosis in activated T cells and, in some contexts, Th17 cells, contributing to reduced inflammation.
- **Adenosine-Mediated Anti-Inflammation**: Accumulation of intracellular metabolites triggers increased extracellular adenosine, which acts on various cell types to suppress inflammation.

These mechanisms collectively reduce immune activation, cytokine production, and histopathological features associated with AD.

---

### Modulation of Immune Pathways

#### 1. Cytokine Regulation

Methotrexate affects both local and systemic cytokine profiles:

| Cytokine           | Expression Change in AD After MTX          | Clinical Impact                                 |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| IL-4               | Decreased (circulating CD4+ memory T cells)| Reduced type-2 immune inflammation              |
| IL-13              | Decreased (circulating CD4+ memory T cells)| Less type-2 polarization and barrier dysfunction |
| IL-31              | Decreased in lesional skin                 | Lowered pruritus, less scratching                |
| IL-31RA            | Increased in epidermis                     | Compensatory receptor upregulation              |
| IL-6, TNF-α        | Minor/no significant change                | Limited direct impact                           |

**Mechanistic Insight:**  
Methotrexate decreases the number of circulating CD4+ memory T cells expressing IL-4 and IL-13, major mediators of type-2 inflammation. It also reduces IL-31 gene expression in lesional skin, directly addressing pruritus—a core symptom of AD. The increase in IL-31RA expression suggests a compensatory mechanism possibly driven by persistent Th2 cytokines.

#### 2. Suppression of Type-2 Immunity

Type-2 cytokine responses drive much of the pathology in AD. MTX, by reducing IL-4 and IL-13 levels, effectively dampens Th2-skewed inflammation, improves epidermal barrier integrity, and lessens downstream chemokine and cytokine production. This translates into clinical improvements in disease severity, as reflected in reduced eczema area and severity scores.

#### 3. JAK/STAT Pathway Inhibition

Many inflammatory cytokines act through the Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) signaling cascades. Research shows methotrexate directly suppresses STAT phosphorylation in human immune cells, even at clinically relevant concentrations. This broad inhibition of JAK/STAT activity dampens signaling downstream of various cytokine receptors, including those for IL-4, IL-13, and others implicated in AD. This mechanism underpins the drug’s effectiveness across multiple inflammatory diseases, including RA and AD.

---

### Immunomodulation and Regulatory T Cells

One of the critical aspects of MTX action is its ability to modulate regulatory T cell (Treg) function, enhancing immune tolerance:

- **Treg Expansion and Function**:  
  MTX administration leads to the restoration of defective Treg function, marked by increased Foxp3 expression—the key transcription factor governing Treg identity and suppressive capacity.
- **Epigenetic Regulation of Foxp3**:  
  By suppressing TAp63, an isoform of p63 that negatively regulates Foxp3, MTX induces hypomethylation of the Foxp3 CNS2 enhancer region, a modification crucial for stable Foxp3 expression. This process increases Treg stability, function, and suppressive capability.
- **Clinical Correlation**:  
  Patients with lower baseline levels of the enzyme CD39 (found on Tregs) show poorer responses to methotrexate, highlighting the link between functional Tregs and efficacy.

---

### Adenosine Signaling Pathway

A key anti-inflammatory mechanism of MTX involves the accumulation and release of adenosine:

- **Adenosine Generation**:  
  Methotrexate increases cellular adenosine monophosphate (AMP) levels via inhibition of ATIC, which is then converted to adenosine extracellularly by CD39 and CD73.
- **Receptor Activation**:  
  Extracellular adenosine binds to A2A receptors on immune cells, triggering anti-inflammatory effects, such as:
    - Inhibition of neutrophil superoxide generation and migration
    - Suppression of macrophage activation and transition toward M2 phenotype
    - Diminished T cell proliferation and enhanced regulatory function
    - Promotion of apoptosis in activated immune cells

Clinical evidence supports this pathway, as caffeine (a nonselective adenosine receptor antagonist) partially blocks the therapeutic effects of methotrexate.

---

### Effects on Skin Histopathology

Methotrexate not only modulates immune cell functions but also alters cutaneous histopathology:

- **Reduction in Epidermal Hyperplasia**:  
  Lesional skin thickness is significantly reduced after methotrexate therapy, indicating decreased keratinocyte proliferation and normalization of skin architecture.
- **Modulation of Pruritus Mediators**:  
  By decreasing IL-31 expression and upregulating IL-31RA, MTX targets the neural and inflammatory pathways that mediate itch—central to patient quality of life in AD.
- **Altered Immune Cell Infiltration**:  
  There is evidence for decreased numbers of pro-inflammatory T helper subsets and decreased overall immune cell recruitment to the skin.

---

### Summary Table: Key Methotrexate Mechanisms in Atopic Dermatitis

| Mechanism                     | Main Effect(s)                                     | Relevance to AD                      |
|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Purine Synthesis Inhibition   | Reduces immune cell proliferation                  | Suppresses activated T cells         |
| Adenosine Release             | Anti-inflammatory signaling via A2A receptors      | Diminishes inflammation and itch     |
| JAK/STAT Pathway Suppression  | Blocks cytokine signaling                         | Dampens IL-4/IL-13/Th2 axis         |
| Treg Enhancement (Foxp3)      | Increases regulatory immune tolerance              | Restores immune balance              |
| Apoptosis Induction           | Eliminates activated immune cells                  | Limits chronic inflammation          |
| IL-4/IL-13 Downregulation     | Curbs type-2 immune response                       | Improves barrier and inflammation  |
| IL-31/IL-31RA Modulation      | Targets pruritus and skin inflammation             | Reduces itch and secondary damage   |

---

### Clinical Implications

Methotrexate is a cornerstone systemic therapy for AD unresponsive to topical treatments and phototherapy. Its multi-pronged approach—targeting both effector and regulatory arms of immunity—makes it effective for disease control, pruritus reduction, and histopathological normalization. The onset of clinical benefit typically occurs within 4–6 weeks, with sustained effects reported over longer durations.

Key clinical considerations include:

- Monitoring for hematologic toxicity (e.g., leukopenia, thrombocytopenia)
- Assessing liver function prior to therapy and periodically during long-term management
- Recognizing potential for infection risk due to broad immunosuppression
- Utilizing supplementation with folic acid to mitigate mucosal and hematologic side effects

---

### Conclusion

Methotrexate ameliorates atopic dermatitis through a multifaceted mechanism: suppression of proliferating and activated immune cells, induction of apoptosis in pathogenic lymphocytes, enhancement of regulatory T cell function, and direct modulation of critical inflammatory pathways. The inhibition of JAK/STAT signaling and adenosine release create a system-wide anti-inflammatory environment, while targeted reductions in Th2 cytokines and pruritogenic mediators address hallmark symptoms of the disease. These integrated actions result in improved clinical outcomes and better quality of life for patients with moderate-to-severe AD.

Future research will continue to refine the molecular and cellular interactions affected by methotrexate, potentially identifying biomarkers for response prediction and strategies for optimizing combination therapies.
